<reflection>
After two experiments with high substrate (1.0 M) and varying catalyst concentrations (0.01 M and 0.05 M), the top mechanisms (M7, M3, M6, M8) remain closely matched in NLL, indicating they are still indistinguishable under these conditions. The second group (M2, M1, etc.) also remains plausible. My aim for the second turn—to amplify differences via higher catalyst concentration—was partially achieved, as the NLL values shifted, but the relative ordering and clustering persisted. To make further progress, we need an experiment that probes a different kinetic regime, specifically one that varies substrate concentration to reveal saturation effects and differential dependencies on [S]. This will help discriminate mechanisms involving multiple substrate binding (M7), dimerization (M3), and activation (M6, M8), as their predicted rate laws respond differently to low substrate.
</reflection>

<hypothesis>
I propose an experiment with low substrate concentration (0.2 M), moderate catalyst (0.01 M), and no product. This design contrasts sharply with the previous high-substrate conditions, moving into a regime where substrate binding saturation becomes significant. Mechanisms like M7 (involving two substrate bindings) may show pronounced curvature or altered apparent order in substrate. Dimer-based mechanisms (M3) may exhibit different effective catalyst orders because dimer equilibrium depends on catalyst concentration, which is held at 0.01 M—low enough that dimer formation might be limited. Activation mechanisms (M6, M8) could display different initial rates if the activation step is influenced by substrate concentration. By testing low substrate, we also probe the linearity of the rate with respect to [S] for simple Michaelis-Menten mechanisms (M1, M2), helping to separate them from more complex models. This condition is informative across many candidates simultaneously, avoiding extreme depletion and preserving mechanistic diversity.
</hypothesis>
